entry.title: Luchino Visconti’s Tragic, Beautiful Final Film ‘L’Innocente’ Restored in 4K — Watch the Trailer
entry.summary: Watch the trailer for the 4K restoration of Italian master filmmaker Luchino Visconti's marital melodrama 'L'Innocente' from 1976.
entry.content:
Luchino Visconti‘s lush, aristocratic worlds have seen a major revival at repertory movie houses over the past year. From the black-and-white “White Nights” with Marcello Mastroianni to the psychosexual queer drama “Conversation Piece” with Burt Lancaster, the Italian grandmaster’s vivid melodramas capture souls adrift, possessive, and tragic. While Visconti is probably best known for epics like “The Leopard” and “Rocco and His Brothers,” in his later career up until his death in 1976, the Palme d’Or-winning filmmaker turned his lens on more intimate dramas and marital discord.

A new restoration of Visconti’s final film, “L’Innocente,” premiered in Cannes Classics and at the New York Film Festival. Starring Giancarlo Giannini, Laura Antonelli, and Jennifer O’Neill, the film was lovingly restored by Film Movement Classics to preserve the film’s 50th anniversary. Below, IndieWire debuts the exclusive trailer for the new release. A theatrical rollout begins December 11.

Related Stories
Watch ‘My Undesirable Friends’ Director Julia Loktev Recall the Week Russia Invaded Ukraine
‘Wildwood’ Sparked a Much-Needed Comeback for Laika at the Box Office

Set in Rome at the turn of the 20th century, the film centers on “a wealthy and self-absorbed nobleman Tullio Hermil (Giancarlo Giannini) [who] carries on an affair with a sophisticated yet possessive widow, Countess Teresa Raffo (Jennifer O’Neill), while treating his devoted wife, Giuliana (Laura Antonelli), with cold condescension. Wounded by his years of neglect, Giuliana takes a lover of her own with young novelist, Filippo (Marc Porel). When she becomes pregnant with Filippo’s child, Tullio’s wounded pride cannot be contained, setting off a chain of events leading to ultimate tragedy.”

The film loosely adapts Gabriele D’Annunzio’s 1892 novel. At the time of production, Visconti had suffered a major stroke a few years prior that didn’t necessarily impact his ability to work, but it made him a liability in terms of securing casting. For “L’Innocente,” Visconti had wanted his “The Leopard” and “Rocco and His Brothers” star, the French actor Alain Delon, in the lead. He also wanted Delon’s ex and repeat Visconti star Romy Schneider in the film, too, as well as Charlotte Rampling (“The Damned”) at one point. Visconti died in March 1976, just two months ahead of the film’s Cannes premiere. Critic Jonathan Rosenbaum called the film “a withering autocritique of masculine vanity and self-delusion.”

Cinelab Service in Italy created a new 4K digital transfer on an Arriscan film scanner, working from the original camera negative.

entry.title: How Two Rival Columnists Created Hollywood’s Gossip Machine — and Taught America to Worship Attention
entry.summary: An excerpt from Eileen Cope's 'Hollywood Whispers: The Untold Story of the Original Gossip Queens, Louella Parsons and Hedda Hopper' charts their rise
entry.content:
In her new book, “Hollywood Whispers: The Untold Story of the Original Gossip Queens, Louella Parsons and Hedda Hopper,” Eileen Cope delves into a rivalry that dramatically shaped the entertainment industry and culture at large throughout the mid-20th century. After the birth of the star system in Hollywood, Parsons and Hopper rose to prominence as gossip columnists who could make and break careers, and choose to keep or expose celebrities’ secrets. With a combined readership of 75 million at their peak, Hopper and Parsons wielded extraordinary influence — and instilled paralyzing fear. As columnist Liz Smith has written, “The studios created both of them. And they thought they could control both of them. But they became Frankenstein monsters escaped from the labs.” In the excerpt below, Cope summarizes their stark differences — and even more striking similarities.

Related Stories
What the Success of ’28 Weeks Later’ Meant for an ‘Indiewood’ Still Finding Its Footing
What’s It Like to Be a Hair and Fur Fabricator for Laika? A New Book Will Answer That (and More)

Hollywood has always been a hall of mirrors. What began as an industry of light and illusion had, by the 1940s, become a machinery of control—an empire built on fantasy, running on fear. Its dreammakers no longer needed scripts or cameras to keep order. They had Louella Parsons and Hedda Hopper.

By then, both women had transcended the ordinary limits of journalism. They were not simply reporters; they were gatekeepers of belief, the quiet regulators of a nation’s imagination. To cross them was to risk vanishing—not merely from the screen, but from the collective story America told about itself.

Hollywood insiders referred to them—half jokingly, half in dread—as “the High Priestesses.” Studio secretaries clipped their columns before the morning dailies reached the lot, marking any mention of the studio’s stars with red pencil. Publicists phoned assistants in panic if a name appeared in the wrong context. “They could wreck you before lunch,” remembered producer Pandro Berman. “And by dinner, they’d make you again—if it suited them.”

It was easy, at first, to mistake their power for personality. Louella, with her sanctimonious charm and the backing of William Randolph Hearst, ruled the studios from her desk at the Los Angeles Examiner. Her typewriter was a throne. Her column ran like clockwork through America’s breakfast tables, a sermon of what was right and who had sinned. Hedda, the actress-turned-crusader, cultivated a different tone—brassy, righteous, vengeful. Her voice carried across radio waves like a call to arms. She didn’t just write gossip; she announced it, her cadence turning every name into an accusation or an absolution.

Both women understood theater. Louella played the role of moral mother, her column written in the soothing cadences of propriety—rarely venomous on the surface, yet devastating in its implications. Hedda was the showwoman. “When she walked into Ciro’s,” recalled gossip photographer Frank Worth, “it was like someone had switched on the lights.” Even those who loathed her found themselves glancing up, afraid she might be looking at them.

Louella and Hedda were two sides of the same coin, minted in a culture that worshipped celebrity and feared moral chaos. Each understood what the studios feared most: scandal, exposure, the sudden rupture of the illusion. And they learned to trade in that fear, turning rumor into regulation.

Louella had built her empire first. By the early 1930s, her column appeared in hundreds of newspapers through the Hearst syndicate, reaching an estimated twenty million readers daily. Hollywood Hotel, her weekly radio show, brought the glamour of opening nights directly into American living rooms. Its mix of studio orchestras, star appearances, and previews of upcoming films created a powerful cycle of cross-promotion: her print column drove listeners to the broadcast, and the broadcast reinforced her authority in print.

She was feared as much as courted. Stars who crossed her found themselves frozen out. Studio executives who annoyed her might find their films receiving tepid coverage. A single line hinting that an actor appeared “unhappy with recent assignments” could trigger studio meetings and contract reviews. Louella’s prose was brief, polite, and devastatingly coded; her readers learned to interpret her tone as carefully as her text. The fear she inspired was not only of what she printed but of what she might choose not to.

The competition she could not have predicted came in the form of a woman she had once treated as a harmless curiosity. By 1935, Hedda Hopper’s film career was essentially over. She was fifty, though she claimed forty-five, watching her savings evaporate and terrified about her future. When a studio executive suggested she could “transition to extra work,” Hedda turned the humiliation into fuel. If she couldn’t star in movies, she would make herself the story. The weapon she would wield was not beauty or youth, but the pen.

When a friend suggested she try writing a gossip column, Hedda was insulted. Writing gossip seemed like a public acknowledgment that she couldn’t make it as a performer. But desperation has a way of making humiliation seem acceptable. She borrowed a typewriter, set up at her kitchen table, and began by writing what she knew best: the petty rivalries of actors who had underestimated her. “I never lied,” she said later, “but I didn’t always tell the truth either.” The early columns were messy but alive, full of energy and vengeance.

Then Hedda got angry. She stopped trying to write like a journalist and started writing like herself— sharp, critical, unsparing, willing to say things other columnists wouldn’t dare print. Twenty years as a working actress had also given her something valuable: relationships with the people Louella ignored. Character actors, crew members, hairdressers, chauffeurs, and wardrobe girls had no loyalty to Louella, and many were happy to talk to Hedda, who had once been one of them.

The Los Angeles Times noticed. Hearst’s primary competitor in Southern California saw Hedda as a weapon against his dominance through Louella. In 1938, the paper offered Hedda a contract with better pay, more resources, and a much larger platform. She would compete directly with the woman who had been Hollywood’s undisputed gossip queen for fifteen years.

Most people thought she would be crushed. Instead, Hedda transformed herself for the opportunity. She began wearing the enormous hats that became her trademark—creations decorated with feathers, flowers, fruit, and even stuffed animals. The hats ensured that everyone at a Hollywood event knew when Hedda Hopper had arrived. She also developed a confrontational style that contrasted with Louella’s cozy approach. Where Louella praised, Hedda criticized. Where Louella protected relationships, Hedda burned bridges. Where Louella sought to be loved, Hedda was content to be feared.

In the beginning, the difference between them seemed simple enough. Louella had the empire; Hedda had the instinct. Louella’s authority came from her link to Hearst—a patriarchal structure she both served and mastered. Hedda’s came from sheer velocity. She moved fast, wrote fast, spoke fast. She had learned that outrage was more contagious than affection.

At first, the two women coexisted uneasily, even politely. Louella sent Hedda a congratulatory telegram when her first radio broadcast went national. Hedda responded with a bouquet of orchids and a note that read, “To the Queen of the Kingdom I am only visiting.” But the civility evaporated as soon as Hedda’s column began pulling readers away from the Examiner. In 1940, when Hedda’s column syndication reached more than six million households, Louella persuaded Hearst’s editors to bar her rival from every Hearst-owned paper.

As the 1940s unfolded, their feud became public theater. Columns answered columns. Louella hinted that Hedda was “overly dramatic.” Hedda fired back, calling Louella “a relic of studio servitude.” Studios courted both women, sometimes feeding them different versions of the same story to see who would publish first. Readers began to choose sides.

In 1945, Photoplay published “Battle of the Typewriters,” complete with caricatures of the two women as dueling queens—Louella seated on a gilt throne, Hedda brandishing her hatpins like weapons. The story outsold every issue that year except the one featuring Clark Gable’s return from the war. The public couldn’t get enough. For a nation recovering from global conflict, the spectacle of two powerful women waging a cold war of words was irresistible.

Their methods echo through the media that followed. The tabloid boom of the 1980s, TMZ, Instagram, celebrity influencers, blind-item accounts, and the daily social-media outrage cycle all trace their lineage to the template Louella and Hedda built. They understood that access could be traded, intimacy manufactured, morality weaponized, and a public image constructed or destroyed through repetition. The machine they built continues to hum behind every red carpet and every scandal recycled for entertainment. What they truly enshrined was attention—and America never stopped worshiping it.

The women themselves could not stop Hollywood from moving on. As the studio system declined and stars emerged, the two gossip queens became relics of the world they had once governed. When the Los Angeles Examiner folded in 1962, Louella suffered a professional blow. Already showing signs of physical deterioration, she nevertheless continued going out, bejeweled and bewildered, like a dowager empress whose country had overthrown her rule. She finally retired in 1965, beset by further medical problems.

Hedda had always advised leaving a party before the glow faded. On February 1, 1966, she died in Los Angeles of double pneumonia at the age of eighty. Her cryptic parting words were entirely in character: “They should know what I haven’t written!”

Louella’s daughter, Harriet, visited her mother at the Santa Monica nursing home to deliver the news that Hedda Hopper was dead. Louella sat in profound silence, then appeared confused. She would live for another six years, largely withdrawn from the world she had once ruled, before dying of arteriosclerosis on December 9, 1972, at the age of ninety-one. But on hearing that her great rival had finally departed, Louella gathered herself long enough to offer one last, unmistakable verdict: “GOOD!”

Adapted from “Hollywood Whispers: The Untold Story of the Original Gossip Queens, Louella Parsons and Hedda Hopper” available November 3 from Lyons Press.

entry.title: Watch ‘My Undesirable Friends’ Director Julia Loktev Recall the Week Russia Invaded Ukraine
entry.summary: Watch 'My Undesirable Friends' director Julia Loktev's appearance at IndieWire's Art of the Doc.
entry.content:
Great documentaries never turn out quite the way you plan them. You might start out thinking that you’re making one film, but a documentarian has to be willing to accept when changes in the lives of their subjects changes the nature of their project.

Julia Loktev‘s two-part documentary “My Undesirable Friends” is a perfect example of this. The films, which follow journalists at TV Rain, which was Russia’s last independent news channel before it was shut down over coverage of the war in Ukraine, began as a story about journalists working in a hostile climate. But when her subjects were forced to flee the country and scatter across Europe, “My Undesirable Friends” had to expand its scale.

Related Stories
‘Wildwood’ Sparked a Much-Needed Comeback for Laika at the Box Office
James Gunn and Peter Safran’s DC Experiment: What’s Working, What Isn’t, and What’s Next

During a conversation with IndieWire’s Chris O’Falt at our Art of the Doc event, Loktev opened up about the project’s origins. While she had already been shooting footage of her subjects, the films truly took shape the week Russia invaded Ukraine.

“Neither of these two films were supposed to happen,” Loktev said. “I just started making a film that I thought was gonna be called ‘The Lives of Foreign Agents’ about these young journalists that were being called foreign agents. And the media were being called undesirable organizations. Of course, what we didn’t know was that four and a half months later, Russia would start a full scale war with Ukraine and shut down all independent media within that first week.”

“‘Part II’ starts right after all these journalists were forced to leave the country,” she continued. “Putin calls them the flies that Russia spits out of its mouth. But that first week was terrifying. Nobody could imagine invading Ukraine. The war had been going for eight years, but it was the kind of year where the world allowed Russia to host a world cup… All of these journalists tried to report the truth to Russians, and up until that moment they were living in Russia. Maybe you were waiting for the police to show up at your office or your home, maybe friends of yours were being arrested, but you could still work in Russia. And then that stopped.”

Watch the complete conversation with Loktev in the video above.

National Geographic Documentary Films, part of a joint venture between The Walt Disney Company and the National Geographic Society, is committed to bringing the world premium, feature documentaries that cover timely, provocative and globally relevant stories from the very best documentary filmmakers. Its award-winning and critically acclaimed films reach 300 million people worldwide in 180 countries and 33 languages across the global National Geographic channels and direct-to-consumer platforms Disney+ and Hulu.

Recent films include the Emmy-nominated winner of the IDA Award for Best Feature “The Tale of Silyan;” Oscar® and Peabody nominee “Sugarcane;” Oscar-nominated and Peabody Award winner “Bobi Wine: The People’s President;” Emmy Award winner “Lost In The Jungle;” Oscar- and BAFTA-nominated “Fire of Love;” Emmy and Peabody Award winner “The Territory;” BAFTA nominees “The Rescue” and “Becoming Cousteau;” and Oscar- and BAFTA winner “Free Solo.” For more information visit films.nationalgeographic.com, or find us on Facebook,Twitter,Instagram, and YouTube.

entry.title: ‘Wildwood’ Sparked a Much-Needed Comeback for Laika at the Box Office
entry.summary: 'Wildwood,' Laika's latest stop-motion animated epic, made $12.2 million domestic at the box office, on par with some of its past hits.
entry.content:
The release of Laika‘s “Wildwood” at the box office this weekend was about more than just the dollars and cents or the success or failure of a single film; in some ways it was about the future of a fan-favorite film studio.

“Wildwood” is the Portland, Oregon-based stop-motion animation studio’s sixth animated feature but also the first movie released by the studio in seven years. Easily director Travis Knight’s most ambitious project to date under the Laika banner, it’s been in the works for even longer than that time gap: fans have been awaiting it for years. Heck, we’ve been talking about this movie since last year.

What Laika needed with “Wildwood” was not just a solid number but a display of genuine enthusiasm that this movie could reintroduce audiences to the studio. Even if a movie like “Coraline,” Laika’s debut, breakout stop-motion hit, was not a gangbusters blockbuster upon its release, it’s a film that has had real staying power and made a legacy for Laika in the process.

Related Stories
James Gunn and Peter Safran’s DC Experiment: What’s Working, What Isn’t, and What’s Next
Laika and Fathom Take Legal Action to Stop ‘Wildwood’ Screenings at L.A.’s Bruin Theatre

“Wildwood” grossed $12.2 million domestic in its opening weekend, placing it at No. 3 for the weekend behind “Clayface” and “You Can See Everything. It also added an additional $2.9 million from a handful of international markets and still has a lot to go. Those aren’t eye-popping numbers, and when you hear reports that the budget is around $100 million, it’s not a surprise that many of the headlines surrounding “Wildwood” are that it could be a big money loser.

But having expensive, hand-crafted passion projects that view budgets as an after-thought are kind of part of Laika’s DNA. And it’s clear after one weekend that “Wildwood” is not the let down its previous feature, 2019’s “Missing Link,” turned out to be. That film opened to less than half of what “Wildwood” did with just $5.9 million and finished at $17 million domestic, a number “Wildwood” will easily surpass.

The better comp for “Wildwood” is “Kubo and the Two Strings,” which opened to $12.6 million and finished with $48 million domestic and $76 million worldwide. It’s also not far off from DreamWorks’ “Forgotten Island” from earlier this year, which opened to $13 million and has made $67.9 million worldwide thus far.

The key though is for “Wildwood” to repeat the stellar holds and word of mouth over time that some of its past hits have done. All five of its previous films have had hefty multiples, including “Coraline” (4.5x), “ParaNorman” (4.1x), and “Kubo and the Two Strings” (3.8x). A 3.8 multiple for “Wildwood,” same as “Kubo,” would have it finish with roughly $46.3 million domestic.

Some of the early exit tracking suggests it has a chance to be even better than that. “Wildwood” received an A CinemaScore and almost universal positive scores and “recommend” grades from PostTrak, in addition to a 99 percent on Rotten Tomatoes at time of writing. It had strong per-screen-averages across 395 PLFs and some Dolby Cinemas in particular, and it even packed houses in places like Portland where the film is set and pays homage.

Dave Burke, Laika’s Chief Marketing Officer and an EP on the film, told IndieWire those figures suggest it could even add a few screens beyond the 2,940 it had this first weekend. Alamo Drafthouse for one played the film on 11 screens and is looking to add another six, Burke said. Also of note is that this is one of Fathom Entertainment’s first truly wide releases for an original film after having big success re-releasing “Coraline,” so both companies are viewing these numbers as encouraging.

“I think we needed to prove ourselves as the new kid on the block, and I think the data points to the fact that there’s a really compelling business case for exhibition to get on even more robustly and support the film in the kind of coming weeks,” Burke said.

Many of Laika’s films have been darker in nature, and “Wildwood” does not shy away from that. The studio has been upfront in its marketing that the film is PG-13, that it aims to reach a general audience rather than kids, and is based on a middlegrade novel from Colin Meloy, better known as the lead singer of the indie folk band The Decemberists. It’s an intense and often violent display of puppetry with a third act that resembles a “Lord of the Rings” war sequence. But even so Burke said the film had a strong showing from the under 34 crowd and a good mix of tweens coming along with their parents. It even received a 5-star grade from the parents’ guide Common Sense Media. These are the types of fans Laika needs to cultivate to get them to revisit their older titles and keep them excited as the company is set to expand into live-action films and whatever other passion project Travis Knight has cooking next.

“People have just really recognized from the get go this is an extraordinary undertaking, and there’s been a real sense that everyone is willing for us to succeed, and I think that is something that we don’t take lightly,” Burke said. “We have a responsibility to make sure that this film gets seen by the widest possible audience, and that’s why I’m so focused on the next couple of weeks, but also its afterlife and what its legacy looks like.”

entry.title: James Gunn and Peter Safran’s DC Experiment: What’s Working, What Isn’t, and What’s Next
entry.summary: After 'Superman,' 'Supergirl,' 'Lanterns,' and 'Clayface,' how is the James Gunn/Peter Safran DC Studios experiment going?
entry.content:
Four years ago this week, James Gunn and Peter Safran were handed one of Hollywood’s most coveted, and impossible, jobs. When they were named co-CEOs of Warner Bros.’ DC Studios label, they received complete oversight of comic book characters like Superman, Wonder Woman, Batman* (more on that later), Green Lantern, the Flash, and countless others. With a seemingly blank canvas to make as many movies and shows as their hearts desired, the implied mandate was clear: get DC Comics out of second place.

The studio’s DC division spent much of the 2010s as a laughingstock while its Marvel competitors seemed to never miss. Despite having a better roster of characters — 20 years ago, mentioning the Guardians of the Galaxy in the same breath as Batman would have been laughable even to the biggest comic book nerd — Warner Bros. couldn’t figure out how to turn its characters into must-see cinema. The incredible cultural moment of the Christopher Nolan Batman movies gave way to one misfire after another: Zack Snyder’s “Man of Steel” gave way to the “Batman v. Superman: Dawn of Justice” debacle, Patty Jenkins’ acclaimed “Wonder Woman” movie led to a critically panned sequel, and the studio’s attempt to launch its own “Avengers” with “Justice League” was bad enough to leave fans arguing about different cuts instead of wondering where the story went next.

Related Stories
Laika and Fathom Take Legal Action to Stop ‘Wildwood’ Screenings at L.A.’s Bruin Theatre
‘Elastic Hearts’ Filmmakers Claim Their Movie Was Denied a Texas Tax Incentive Over Abortion Storyline

It was the kind of turnaround project that entitles its leaders to a long runway. After Gunn and Safran accepted the job in late 2022, they began announcing projects in early 2023. Then they had to shoot and edit them, meaning that we didn’t really see the vision take shape until this year. But now we’ve seen Gunn and Safran release three major theatrical films, two live-action shows, and multiple animated ones — more than enough of a sample size to start grading their creative direction. Even if we’re still in Phase One of their long-term plan, the pros and cons of their studio approach are becoming clear.

The Films

Gunn and Safran kicked off their DC tenure with the safest and smartest film they could have possibly made: a “Superman” movie written and directed by Gunn himself. Putting DC’s signature character in the hands of a filmmaker with an unimpeachable ability to deliver smart popcorn fare was a no-brainer. And in many ways, “Superman” delivered.

The film wisely skipped the obligatory origin story that everyone already knows, checking in with the man formerly known as Kal-El after he had already assumed his dual role of Superman and Clark Kent on Earth. Gunn brought his signature blend of heart, humor, and needle drops, delivering an entertaining blockbuster that stood in clear contrast to the excessively dark DC films of the 2010s. This movie was colorful and fun, even in its heaviest moments. Unsurprisingly, it grossed over $600 million worldwide — though it still didn’t tell us much about Gunn’s ability to run a studio. His bona fides as a comic book writer/director were never in doubt, but we still hadn’t seen him supervise other filmmakers.

Those opportunities came in 2026, and the results were more polarizing. The studio’s second film, “Supergirl,” was one of the year’s most public flops. Milly Alcock’s eponymous character appeared briefly in “Superman,” but Craig Gillespie’s film traded its predecessor’s grounded Earth drama for a space western set across a series of “Mad Max”-esque planets. The confusing mythology and grating visual effects felt like a departure, and the film received mixed reviews and only made $100 million worldwide despite costing nearly twice that. Equally concerning were reports about creative clashes between Gunn and Safran and Gillespie, with two competing cuts being screened against each other months before the movie opened.

Then came “Clayface.” James Watkins’ origin story for an obscure Batman villain was branded as a horror movie that just happened to exist within a comic book universe. The gory, goopy story of an actor who sacrifices everything to regain his skin-deep beauty wasn’t for everyone, but it represented a real creative swing. And it was made on a responsible $44 million budget, which removed the pressure to be universally appealing.

It’s easy to see a world where this DC universe thrives with a combination of major tentpoles directed by Gunn (who is already hard at work on a “Superman” follow-up dated for July 2027) and smaller, weirder films based on minor characters. But we still haven’t seen Gunn and Safran oversee a blockbuster that connects with mainstream audiences with another filmmaker in the director’s chair. “Supergirl” may end up being an anomaly, but right now it still represents one-third of their theatrical output. That sadly has to count for something.

Grade: B–

The Shows

Gunn and Safran’s overhaul of DC’s TV output technically began before they took over as CEOs, as “Peacemaker” premiered on HBO Max nine months earlier. Created (and largely directed) by Gunn, the raunchy action comedy saw John Cena reprising his role from Gunn’s “Suicide Squad” movie as an antihero willing to kill as many men, women, and children as he needs to achieve his goal of world peace. Gunn’s sensibilities were still there, but the HBO brand let the show include far more nudity and profanity than you’d ever find in a four-quadrant film. A hit with fans and critics, “Peacemaker” reminded audiences what was possible when you had access to a premium cable brand to complement your theatrical films.

Their first official project after taking the reins was also a TV show. The animated “Creature Commandos” debuted on HBO Max in December 2024 with an inoffensive six-episode Season 1 that showcased Gunn’s favorite themes about weirdos who assemble their own found families. The business stakes were low — fairly or not, the average consumer isn’t watching animated superhero shows, and the diehard fans who do tune in are unlikely to ever stop supporting DC’s other projects. But the series has one notable wrinkle: Gunn cast its voice actors with the intention of reprising their roles in live-action projects, a tactic he says he plans to use on all future animated projects.

“Peacemaker” also concluded with a well-received Season 2, but the real test of the DC Universe’s TV output came this fall with “Lanterns.” Chris Mundy, Damon Lindelof, and Tom King’s series about DC’s intergalactic police force more than delivered on its promise to be “True Detective” with Green Lanterns. The film uses classic police procedural tropes — the show centers on an older, set-in-his-ways Green Lantern who reluctantly partners with a talented young partner he won’t give the time of day to — in a dark, season-long murder saga set in middle America. The show itself received rave reviews, but its actual contents matter less than what it represents: a unique, auteur-driven project that fits into Gunn and Safran’s storyline while allowing other filmmakers to showcase their own voices. So far, it’s the ultimate example of what the CEOs have always said they wanted their DC Studios to do.

Grade: A-

The Batman Problem

Perhaps the biggest variable facing Gunn and Safran’s DC Studios is largely outside their control. Matt Reeves’ “The Batman” had already opened in theaters a few months before they took over, and Warner Bros. announced that the Robert Pattinson-led series would continue separately from the new DC Universe. A second film is in production, with Steven Soderbergh helping to complete principal photography, and HBO shows like “The Penguin” and the recently announced “Poison Ivy” continue to expand the mythology.

Gunn and Safran have some involvement in these “Batman” projects and publicly support them, but the films and shows exist outside the overarching storyline they’re trying to build. And while it’s not an insurmountable problem — multiple artists working with the same characters in different timelines has been a trademark of comic books from the very beginning — it’s also not ideal to have one of your franchise’s two biggest characters tied up outside your purview.

Nothing’s stopping Gunn and Safran from bringing in their own Batman, and it seems inevitable that it will happen soon. “Clayface” takes place in Gotham City, and once you start introducing Batman villains, you need to give audiences something to fight them. Gunn and Safran previously tapped Andy Muschietti to direct a Batman movie called “The Brave and the Bold,” which was still in development as of 2025, but no cast or release date has been announced.

Many fans and Warner Bros. shareholders believe this DC Universe won’t reach its full potential until it introduces its own Batman. The kind of major team-up movies with billion-dollar box office potential, like a new “Justice League” or a “World’s Finest” team-up between Batman and Superman, all feature the Dark Knight. And assuming their Batman isn’t Robert Pattinson, they’ll inevitably be faced with audiences who wonder why or see theirs as a second-tier product.

It’s not fair to grade Gunn and Safran on this problem, since they didn’t create it, but they still have to navigate it. Again, it’s not insurmountable, but Kevin Feige never had to deal with this at Marvel.

Grade: N/A

The Process

Gunn and Safran’s overarching DC story is still in its infancy, but their development process has become clear. And it’s arguably their best asset. In many ways, their DC Studios can be described as the anti-MCU. Whereas their competitor (and Gunn’s former employer) became famous for seeing everything as part of a larger puzzle, DC Studios seems much more focused on treating each film as a standalone project. Films are greenlit based on the quality of their individual scripts, not the Easter eggs that connect them. Nobody would ever tell you that a brand-new DC cinematic universe should release “Clayface” as one of its first films, but Gunn has openly said Mike Flanagan’s script stood out among the many other projects they were developing. The script was ready; therefore, they made the movie.

Prioritizing scripts over corporate synergy should be music to the ears of cinephiles burned out on Marvel’s assembly-line approach to storytelling. That means continuity will never be as tight as what you find in the MCU, and plenty of projects will be announced without ever coming to fruition. (We’re still upset about James Mangold’s “Swamp Thing” and Luca Guadagnino’s “Sgt. Rock” falling through the cracks, but it’s better than rushing out movies that aren’t ready.) Comic book fans used to following these companies like sports teams might need to adjust their expectations, but movie lovers who care less about those details should get richer viewing experiences. It’s also better for the creatives who get a chance to pitch their own original ideas and put their own stamp on beloved characters.

The only thing holding this back from an “A” grade is the fact that ideals that sound good on paper still have to be executed. I deeply admire Gunn for publicly declaring that no DC Studios movie will receive a release date until everyone is happy with the script. But I also saw “Supergirl” and wondered what this mysterious great script could have possibly looked like, and why it apparently didn’t make it into the finished movie.

Grade: B+

entry.title: Laika and Fathom Take Legal Action to Stop ‘Wildwood’ Screenings at L.A.’s Bruin Theatre
entry.summary: Laika and Fathom tell IndieWire they're seeking to halt 'Wildwood' screenings at L.A.’s Bruin Theatre, citing concerns about operator Rui Pereira.
entry.content:
L.A.’s historic Bruin Theatre met its ambitious fall reopening target on Friday, October 23, but its return is already facing a challenge from the companies behind its first attraction. Laika and Fathom Entertainment say they have taken legal action to stop the Bruin from showing “Wildwood.”

The film was previously advertised as a week-long run at the newly reopened Westwood venue. But in a joint statement provided exclusively to IndieWire, the animation studio and its theatrical distribution partner said concerns about operator Rui Pereira‘s history of controversial comments and behavior prompted them to seek an end to screenings.

Related Stories
‘Elastic Hearts’ Filmmakers Claim Their Movie Was Denied a Texas Tax Incentive Over Abortion Storyline
Why Emmy Wins and Hollywood Recognition Don’t Guarantee Jobs for BIPOC Artists: ‘The Needle Has Not F***ing Moved’

“When Laika became aware of the Bruin engagement, we immediately raised concerns with Fathom Entertainment, our theatrical distribution partner. Laika and Fathom commenced legal action to end the film’s screenings at the theatre,” the companies said in an email.

“We have not yet received confirmation that the screenings have stopped. We are continuing to explore our options, as the concerns regarding the theatre operator are incompatible with the values of our two companies.” IndieWire independently confirmed that “Wildwood” screenings had continued at the Bruin through at least Sunday afternoon, October 25, and as of publication, the theater’s website still advertised daily screenings at 1:30 p.m., 4 p.m., 7 p.m., and 9:30 p.m.

Laika and Fathom Entertainment did not specify what kind of legal action they had taken to stop showings of their film. On a phone call with IndieWire, Pereira asked how we had obtained a cease-and-desist letter. IndieWire had neither received nor reviewed such a letter and told Pereira we had communicated directly with the companies. He continued, “You guys are assholes. Everything you have written is false.”

The dispute introduces an immediate programming problem for Pereira’s revived movie palace, which reopened with “Wildwood” after sitting dark since Regency Theatres departed the space in July 2024. It also follows months of scrutiny involving Pereira, whose rocky history operating Toronto’s Kingsway Theatre became the subject of an IndieWire investigation on September 3.

IndieWire’s earlier reporting examined allegations of assault, nonpayment, racial discrimination, online harassment, and unauthorized film exhibition. The reporting drew on interviews with more than 25 sources in the U.S. and Canada, as well as court records, digital correspondence, social media posts, and years of advertised Kingsway screenings some rights holders say they did not authorize. Pereira has broadly disputed those allegations and characterized the ongoing scrutiny of his businesses as an effort to undermine his work as an exhibitor.

“There are no controversies and any attempt to generate them is dishonest and disingenuous,” Pereira said then. “The Bruin Theater is a gift, not only to Los Angeles, but the world — a cultural heritage site that unites generations of movie goers in the experience of cinema.”

Several journalists have described being targeted by Pereira after publishing critical coverage or omitting the Kingsway from their reporting. Speaking with IndieWire on the phone and in a subsequent email on October 26, Pereira referred to IndieWire staff as “presstitutes” and accused the publication of getting paid to write about him negatively.

Two volunteers left the Bruin restoration project in August after posts attributed to the Kingsway account circulated among Los Angeles moviegoers. Screenshots reviewed by IndieWire included racist and antisemitic remarks, as well as exchanges targeting individual patrons. Sources also described threats and a pattern of prolonged retaliation, alleging that Pereira continued targeting some critics online for months or years after their initial disputes.

When asked by The Hollywood Reporter in an August 23 report about some specific Kingsway posts — including one telling a target to “Go back to Poland” and another describing a swastika painted on a Jewish family’s home as “the proper symbol for zionazis” — Pereira acknowledged that the comments were “offensive” and said he “must take responsibility.”

The current dispute over “Wildwood” also follows separate questions about the Kingsway’s programming. IndieWire previously identified 55 advertised screenings of 17 films that three rights holders said they had not authorized at Pereira’s Toronto theater. Those findings came from a limited sample and did not establish that all or even most Kingsway screenings were unlicensed. “There are no issues with film licensing or any disputes,” Pereira said previously.

Notably, Laika and Fathom’s statement does not suggest that the Bruin’s “Wildwood” booking was unauthorized from the outset. Rather, the companies say they sought to end the Bruin screenings over specific concerns about Pereira as operator. “Wildwood” opened in nearly 3,000 theaters nationwide, and a booking on that scale is hardly an endorsement of every exhibitor.

Still, independent theaters often build their identities around the taste and reputations of the people running them. At a beloved landmark like the Bruin, affection for an old movie palace can translate into intense trust in whoever promises to save it. For now, the location has achieved the reopening its new operator promised. Whether it can continue showing the film that brought audiences back is in dispute.

entry.title: ‘Elastic Hearts’ Filmmakers Claim Their Movie Was Denied a Texas Tax Incentive Over Abortion Storyline
entry.summary: Indie film 'Elastic Hearts' was denied a tax credit after filming in Texas over what the filmmakers claim were political reasons tied to abortion.
entry.content:
Filmmaker Milad Avaz hoped his movie might ruffle some feathers and start a conversation, but he never expected it would create controversy as he was making it.

Avaz is a Danish-Iranian filmmaker based out of Copenhagen who last year shot his first English-language feature titled “Elastic Hearts.” The indie film stars Cole Sprouse, Darby Lee-Stack, Dean Norris, and Stephen Dorff, and after experiencing how many films are always fighting for competition in Los Angeles, he and his brother, producer Misam Avaz, decided to shoot somewhere else: Texas.

The location made narrative sense, too. The film follows a 19-year-old cello prodigy living in a rural part of Texas who turns to her gay, estranged older brother for help when she discovers she’s pregnant. That prompts the two of them to travel out of state to visit an abortion clinic. But “Elastic Hearts” is more concerned with grief and family coming together than abortion rights in Texas, where the procedure has been largely outlawed since 2022.

Related Stories
Why Emmy Wins and Hollywood Recognition Don’t Guarantee Jobs for BIPOC Artists: ‘The Needle Has Not F***ing Moved’
From ‘The Devils’ to ‘Obsession,’ How ‘Femcel’ Horror Handles Horny Women

The Avaz brothers were not naive to that fact when they chose Texas as a shooting location and when they applied for a grant through the Texas Moving Image Industry Incentive Program (TMIIIP), which can net filmmakers up to a 31 percent tax credit in grant money for eligible productions. They were also not naive to Texas rules for eligibility, which award grant funds after production, not before, and which explicitly state that the Texas Film Commission may deny any application “because of inappropriate content or content that portrays Texas or Texans in a negative fashion.” But after working closely with the Texas Film Commission and Austin Film Commission for months during pre-production, they thought the credit was a sure thing.

So they were shocked to learn that after an abnormally long delay, their application was rejected; no formal reason was given in writing. Avaz claims, though, that in a subsequent call with someone at the film commission who was equally shocked, he and his brother say “Elastic Hearts” was denied a grant for political reasons following a closed-door meeting directly from the office of Texas Governor Greg Abbott. It was what was said to them at the end of the call that floored them most.

“You made a film about abortions in Texas. What did you expect?”

“It was so blatant that political influence and government elected officials had an influence on what art was being created that we were just baffled by it,” Milad Avaz told IndieWire exclusively. “I definitely think that’s why it was denied. So when you ask me, what do you think are the themes that led to this, I can tell you pretty upfront that it’s the abortion rights.”

Texas’ film credit program has very recently become a political football after a Texas House representative called the program a “socialist scheme” and vowed to repeal it after a star of “The Chosen” endorsed Democrat James Talarico in the looming U.S. Senate election. It’s also not the first time the Texas Film Commission has denied a credit. In 2019, Robert Rodriguez (who is about as Texan as it gets) unsuccessfully sued after his application for a grant on “Machete Kills” was twice denied.

What makes the case of “Elastic Hearts” shocking though, is how an indie film that used a largely Texan crew was not just denied but had the rug pulled out from under them after the movie was completed. Avaz feels his rejection is a chilling example of what can happen when politics influences art.

“I’m not naive. I know the outcome of this decision fits very well with the political climate, both in America and in the world right now. I just do not think we should be okay with this,” Avaz said. “I don’t think this should be something that, oh well, this is the time where political leaders decide what art is made, so we’re not going to really focus on it. This needs to be documented that we live in a time where, in our industry that is really struggling in a lot of ways, we also have to deal with the very little money available for us independent filmmakers being withheld for political reasons. We have some of our heroes in the film industry doing commercials for ‘Come to Texas, film here!’ Just don’t make it political in any way.”

“It shouldn’t be like this when you do movies,” Milad’s brother Misam Avaz said. “As a movie maker, you should have the right when you use your voice to tell something this important, you should have that freedom of speech. I think it’s a thing that we need to do something about. I asked Milad, and he had the same feeling that I had in the guts, this is not right.”

“Elastic Hearts” carried a $2.2 million budget, and the film’s application, which was filed ahead of the film’s start of production on September 8, 2025, outlined an estimated $1.24 million in planned Texas spending (Avaz said the spending was closer to $1.3 million). Avaz was informed the turnaround time for the application generally lasts 1-3 months, but they did not receive a formal response until nine months later on June 25, 2026, well after production in Texas had wrapped. The film has now already completed post-production and has submitted for consideration at Sundance and South By Southwest (if Avaz is allowed back in the state after this incident, he jokes).

Avaz described the formal response via email, which IndieWire has obtained, as vague and succinct to the point that it felt like they were canceling lunch plans, not rejecting a grant worth over a hundred thousand dollars. When the application was denied and they asked for an explanation, Avaz found them unwilling to supply a reason in writing. It was not until August that they were able to get their representative from the Texas Film Commission to speak to them on the phone, at which point they were told the governor’s office reviewed the film for its political content as part of a closed-door meeting at which their rep was not permitted. When asked if they could appeal or apply again, they were told it wouldn’t make a difference.

In a statement to IndieWire, Governor Abbott’s Press Secretary Andrew Mahaleris said, “Under Texas law, the office is not required to act on every grant application and reviews each application thoroughly. In making determinations, the office considers general standards of decency and respect for the diverse beliefs and values of the citizens of Texas. The State does not use taxpayer dollars to fund projects that portray Texas or Texans in a negative fashion.”

The written application for “Elastic Hearts” does not explicitly mention abortion as part of the film’s story but describes the film as about two siblings who, “haunted by the recent loss of their mother, and carrying the weight of unresolved grief, the two navigate a fractured relationship marked by love, guilt, and buried pain. As they move through dusty towns, desert highways, and chance encounters with strangers, the journey forces them to confront the past and redefine their sense of family.”

The application does note, however, that in addition to hiring a local crew of 40+ people, as well as about 125 background actors, “Elastic Hearts” is a “tribute to and reimagining of Texas,” one that, with some international distribution deals already secured, will have a global reach for the state’s tourism.

“The film captures the textures of rural towns, long desert roads, neon-lit motels, and the quiet strength found in the everyday rhythms of the state. With locations ranging from Elgin to beautifully made minimalistic churches, Texas becomes more than a backdrop. It is woven into the emotional and visual fabric of the story,” the application reads in part. “Texas is not just a backdrop but a central part of the film’s emotional and visual identity, influencing the tone, atmosphere, and character relationships throughout the story.”

Avaz argued too that the film’s story isn’t black and white in its ideas about abortion. It’s a movie about a young woman making a difficult decision because she knows either choice — to keep the child or terminate the pregnancy — might be right for her.

“I needed to show this place from a place of love. There was no way this was going to represent Texas in a wrong light or in a negative way because I didn’t view Texas in a negative way,” he said. “I love the place. Me and my family lived there for half a year, and we want to go back. The response I also got from the crew was that we’re doing something they felt was important and they could really stand behind this project.”

“Elastic Hearts” stood to earn a credit of about $128,000, according to Misam, which came from a base credit of 10 percent based on their amount of spend, as well as a small additional credit for shooting in rural locations. The money would’ve effectively covered the post-production budget, and as a result it hurts the backend they can earn from this film and impacts their ability to start on the next project on their slate. They’re stable as a company after this, but it easily could be something that would ruin another filmmaker or first-time director.

Avaz said everyone involved was riled up based on the decision, and in statements to IndieWire, both of the stars Sprouse and Lee-Stack made that outrage clear.

“By all criteria our film qualified for the state’s film incentive, and if what we’ve been told is true, then the denial of our application is a constitutional violation of the First Amendment and more plainly — viewpoint discrimination,” Sprouse said. “Our jobs as artists often intersect with existing social and political boundaries, and it’s our duty to fight against the erasure of those suffering within this broken system. If the news of denial on these grounds is legitimate, then I’m deeply disappointed by both the cowardice of the Texas Film Commission and not surprised in the slightest by Governor Abbott.”

“Censorship. That is what it says. This is yet another attempt to control our freedom of choice and speech in the U.S,” Lee-Stack added. “This decision made by one politician on behalf of all Texans robs Texas of an opportunity to represent itself as a community of diverse thought and culture. This film is not just about one issue. At the core of ‘Elastic Hearts’ is a reflection of the state’s natural beauty and the admirable resilience of its people. Independent film — the epitome of our freedom of speech and self-expression — should not be controlled by politicians. Regardless of this attempt, I believe this film will reach who it needs to reach because it is too relevant and necessary to be stifled.”

entry.title: Why Emmy Wins and Hollywood Recognition Don’t Guarantee Jobs for BIPOC Artists: ‘The Needle Has Not F***ing Moved’
entry.summary: IndieWire talks to BIPOC talent below- and above-the-line to address the opportunity gaps in Hollywood.
entry.content:
Get the agent, book the studio job, win the award, and so on, collecting infinity stones like Thanos until you can buy that dream house in that quaint part of Studio City. For many working filmmakers, especially women and people of color, the realities of making it in Hollywood are even more nuanced. Recognition can get you into the room, but it does not necessarily get your movie made.

Bridget Stokes knows this distinction intimately. When she became the first Black woman to win an Emmy for directing a variety series in 2022 (“A Black Lady Sketch Show”), meetings followed, and congratulations poured in from every angle. She says the award may have earned her more sit-downs when she reached out, but it didn’t produce the career acceleration outsiders might expect. “I didn’t get a [studio] job offer for almost four years after I had won the award,” Stokes said. “Like four years after I had won an Emmy and had this decoration, I never got a job offer.”

Related Stories
From ‘The Devils’ to ‘Obsession,’ How ‘Femcel’ Horror Handles Horny Women
Walter Koenig, Actor Who Played Chekov on ‘Star Trek,’ Dies at 90

Her experience comes amid a contraction that has made an already difficult business considerably harder. According to a Film LA 2025 Q4 and year-to-date Film Production Report, Los Angeles on-location production fell 16.1 percent in 2025. Every major category declined, including student films, shorts, documentaries, and music videos. At the end of 2025, television production was 50.1 percent below its five-year average and feature films were 31.7 percent below.

The coronavirus pandemic, major labor strikes in the entertainment and media industry, mega mergers like Skydance, and the 2025 wildfires have played a major role in these declines. Though Film LA’s 2026 Q1 report shows an uptick from recent lows, production remains far below historical levels.

“There’s No Place You Can Reach and Have Made It”

Stokes’ experience also complicates one of Hollywood’s most enduring ideas about success — that it’s linear, and that careers operate like ladders. Climb high enough and eventually you reach a level where getting the next project greenlit becomes easier. “There’s no place you can reach and have made it,” Stokes said. She has spoken with Oscar-nominated directors and established auteurs who still struggle to finance passion projects. “We’re artists trying to convince commerce people to make our art. It’s just never going to be easy, no matter who you are.” Stokes wrote and will direct her upcoming project “Zugzwang,” a film noir political thriller starring Christina Elmore as Lady, a Black female private detective and former child soldier.

Who originates the work can tell you who will get the jobs. In her 2026 report, Boxed In, author Martha M. Lauzen of the Center for the Study of Women in Television and Film at San Diego University, found that programs with at least one woman creator employed substantially more women in other key creative positions. Women wrote 48 percent of episodes on those programs, compared with just 17 percent on programs created exclusively by men. The report says women accounted for just 22 percent of creators across broadcast and streaming television in the 2025-26 season.

These pressures are creating a new slate of indie filmmakers who aren’t posting eulogies to Hollywood on Threads or waiting for the good old days to return. They are finding investors, building production companies, making smaller projects, cultivating core audiences and collaborating with one another. In some cases, they are questioning whether the traditional markers of Hollywood success should remain the destination at all.

Producer Ebony Elaine Hardin has spent enough time inside both systems to see the contrast. Hardin began in casting, working for companies including CBS and NBCUniversal and casting directors Francine Maisler and Carmen Cuba before moving into production. Today, she is director of production at Dropout, an independent, subscriber-funded comedy network, studio, and distributor.

“We kind of dropped out of the studio system,” Hardin said tongue-in-cheek. Instead of trying to meet the expectations of a larger corporate owner, the company chose something smaller, more creatively autonomous, and able to craft programs for its audience.

That model challenges another assumption of the traditional system. Must everything appeal to everybody in order to be successful? “I don’t think that entertainment personally has to do that,” Hardin said. “It can be more niche.” She said the independent model can start with a smaller community. “This is just for these people,” made by people who care deeply about that audience. If the work eventually crosses over, all the better.

In 2025, just one in 10 of Hollywood’s top theatrical films had a woman director, while roughly one in five had a director of color, according to UCLA’s 2026 Hollywood Diversity Report for theatrical feature films. The numbers get worse when you count all credited writers. BIPOC writers accounted for just 13.5 percent of the 185 writers for top theatrical releases, while women accounted for 19.5 percent. 71.9 percent of all credited writers were white men.

Vietnam-born actor Trieu Tran, who immigrated to Canada and was raised in Boston, has been working professionally for 25 years. He said this year marked his first time working with a Vietnamese filmmaker. He has worked on cult classics like “How High” and “Tropic Thunder,” spent two-and-a-half seasons on HBO’s “The Newsroom,” built a substantial theater career in such works as “Equus,” where he played Alan Strang alongside East West Players co-star George Takei, earning a Los Angeles Drama Critics Circle (LADCC) nomination, and even once flew to Thailand for the independent feature “Trade of Innocence” opposite Oscar-winning actress Mira Sorvino in 2011.

The film gave him a prominent supporting role as Duke, the antagonist. “I’m in Thailand with Dermot Mulroney and Mira Sorvino. The three of us, making this film for two months. I’m thinking, hey, you know, now here’s my chance,” Tran recalled. He returned home hoping the film would succeed, but it didn’t find its audience. “You come back, and the film was not a success for myriads of reasons,” Tran said.

He had no clear next steps to take. “I’m booking the jobs. All my coworkers are telling me I’m a good actor. I do theater. All the critics are loving my work. Audiences are loving my work, and I’m just like, I don’t know what I need to do to get to that next sort of level, and then ‘The Newsroom’ happened.” After the 2012 Aaron Sorkin series, Tran worked on S1 of “Altered Carbon” as series regular “Mr. Leung” in 2018, and then starred as “Sharko” in Hulu’s 2020 anthology “Monsterland.”

In a SYFY WIRE interview, show creator, executive producer and writer Mary Laws said of Tran, “I think that he’s a phenomenal actor who just has not gotten his day and I think that that’s part of the inherent racism in Hollywood. And we, as a writers’ room, fought really hard to make sure that we cast a Vietnamese actor in that role as a Vietnamese trawler.” Since the show, Tran hasn’t had any acting work — in film or TV — outside of theater.

The Needle Only Moves for a Select Few

To be clear, making a living as an artist is precarious for actors of any race. But actors of color, Tran said, start with a bigger mountain to climb, with fewer roles available and many still constrained by stereotypes. Casting feedback can become almost absurdly specific: “Too Asian, not Asian enough. Too Vietnamese, not Vietnamese enough,” he said. “I hate when I hear people say the needle is moving. The needle has not fucking moved. We need to stop saying that. It’s only moving for a select few.”

BIPOC performers made up only 23.1 percent of leads in top theatrical films in 2025 despite comprising 45.2 percent of the U.S. population, according to UCLA’s report. Asian actors made up just 3.7 percent of that lead slice. When young actors ask Tran for advice, he tells them, “There is literally no blueprint. There’s luck involved…not quitting, getting the opportunity, and finally getting the sheer luck. There’s so many intangibles why you get cast and don’t cast. And a lot of time, it really has nothing to do with talent.”

Emmy-winning casting director Jazzy Collins has watched the traditional markers of achievement lose some of their predictive power. She is the first Black woman to win the Emmy for Outstanding Reality Casting. She said an award gives her name “a little bit more weight,” particularly among people accustomed to the traditional Hollywood hierarchy. But she has also watched digital creators build lucrative careers without ever appearing on a network television show.

“There’s some really fantastic people that have never won an Oscar, never won an Emmy, and they’re working more than the people that have,” Collins said. She isn’t dismissive of those honors. “I am so thankful for it,” she said of her own recognition. Rather, she believes the traditional markers of what makes you good in this industry are changing.

“This Hustle Doesn’t Stop Just Because You Meet Five Investors”

So Collins has spent years learning another, rarely romanticized part of filmmaking: fundraising. She has deliberately sought out investors, learned how to discuss financial structures, and built relationships with people interested in financing films. Work that, she said, never really ends. “This hustle doesn’t stop just because you meet five investors,” Collins said. In doing that work, she arrived at her current philosophy, “I’m not gonna wait for you to knock on my door. You’re gonna have to come knock on my door when I’m already up and running.”

Filmmaker Lauri Levenfeld shares the same sentiment. “I’ve always been extremely scrappy and known that I’ve got to participate in many ways to make a project happen,” said the writer-director who got her start in film as a cinematographer. Levenfeld will direct her feature “Swipe Up,” a southern-gothic horror dark comedy about a deadly sorority competition, while also producing Stokes’ “Zugzwang.” For emerging filmmakers, Levenfeld argues, a good script and financing aren’t enough. “You have to literally think about from A to Z how you’re going to get this thing done.”

Former Netflix executive and producer Wayne Horton offers an important counterweight to the romance of going independent. “Studios have become increasingly risk-averse,” he said, “because executives are under enormous pressure to make projects that work.” Familiar stars and proven filmmakers offer some protection against that risk, but the result can be fewer opportunities for people without many credits. Independent filmmakers cannot ignore those economics either.

“There are a lot of great scripts out there, but there isn’t a strong business case for every script,” Horton said. “My job as a producer is to develop projects that are great creatively, but also turn a profit.” With so many entertainment options, viewers have become extremely segmented. To have a sustainable career in this business, Horton said, he has to develop work that speaks directly to specific audiences. Horton is developing several projects, including a high school rom-com starring Marsai Martin and an ensemble comedy with Emmy winner Lamorne Morris attached.

Is the Answer in Indies?

The data suggests these audiences are a big part of the business. BIPOC moviegoers bought the majority of opening-weekend tickets for five of the top 10 and 11 of the top 20 films at the global box office in 2025, plus half the tickets for another film, according to the UCLA report, and the theatrical films with casts that were 41–50 percent BIPOC produced the highest median global and domestic box office.

And filmmakers building outside Hollywood’s traditional gates aren’t rejecting the business. Increasingly, they are learning more of it themselves. Who is the audience? How much should the film cost? Where does the financing come from? How will people find it? And the question most recently making headlines: Who owns what they create?

Hardin once viewed success through traditional Hollywood milestones, but now has a broader sense of what a creative career looks like. These days she’s more focused on making work she cares about with a community she wants to work alongside.

“I know incredibly talented writers and directors with phenomenal stories,” she said. And as creative producer and executive at her company 903 Entertainment, she’s championing “Flacalta Effect,” a satirical zombie movie in which an Ozempic-like drug triggers a zombie apocalypse, written and directed by Rochae Jeffrey and featuring an all-POC cast, and “Trashy People,” a coming-of-age story about a young woman working at her college recycling center to pay for school, written and directed by Marissa High.

Hardin hasn’t given up on the accolades either. She still wants the Emmy. She still submits projects to Sundance and SXSW. She still intends to knock on those doors, but no longer believes she has to wait behind them. “I’m just going to keep knocking until I get my moment,” Hardin said. A moment she’s certain will come through independent work.

And the data supports her confidence. According to feature film data from Film LA’s Q1 2026 production report, feature production rose 52.3 percent year over year in Q1 2026, from 451 to 687 shoot days, and was actually 20.6 percent above the five-year average. Most of that quarter’s feature-film activity came from independent films.

The revolution will likely be built on an indie budget (including equitable backend for all involved), and it just might get a theatrical release before it goes to streaming. The heavily guarded industry gates will likely never fling open, but with filmmakers now understanding exactly how high the mountain is, they are much better poised to build another path up.

Chaseedaw Giles is a Los Angeles-based journalist, screenwriter, and filmmaker.

entry.title: From ‘The Devils’ to ‘Obsession,’ How ‘Femcel’ Horror Handles Horny Women
entry.summary: Horror has always been fearfully fascinated with female desire. Now, offscreen, women are questioning whether real romance is worth wanting at all.
entry.content:
Has sexual violence always been a spectator sport? It certainly has an audience. Last week, prediction market Polymarket removed a contract that allowed users to bet on whether any of the seven men accused of sexually assaulting a Cornell University student in an alleged gang rape would face felony sex-crime charges.

The men have broadly denied the allegations, and no one has been criminally charged. But before the Polymarket contract came down, bets about the Cornell case generated more than $450,000 in trading volume — suggesting that just the prospect of accountability for claims of alleged sexual violence can be repackaged and sold as dark entertainment today.

Related Stories
Walter Koenig, Actor Who Played Chekov on ‘Star Trek,’ Dies at 90
How ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York’ Used Vintage ‘Godfather’ Lenses to Capture NYC on Location

Ken Russell’s “The Devils” understood the power of that spectacle 55 years ago. Now enjoying an extended theatrical run following its long-awaited restoration, the notorious 1971 film reveals how readily powerful institutions can turn women’s private experiences into public theater. In Russell’s feverish account of religious repression, a nun’s unrequited lust for a priest becomes a political weapon: a message that’s only grown more resonant in an era of increasing cruelty online.

In the decades since, horror hasn’t stopped asking what happens when women want too much. If anything, the cultural fascination with female rage has made those questions more urgent and their resolutions more complicated. From Curry Barker’s “Obsession” to Jane Schoenbrun’s “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,” this year has produced a striking collection of women whose desires — and other people’s attempts to control them — become sources of terror, humiliation, and transformation.

The internet’s evolving concept of the “femcel” label offers a provocative lens through which to reconsider these characters, even if none fits its original definition of a woman denied romantic or sexual satisfaction particularly well. Offscreen, meanwhile, women are asking another question: What if the intimate relationships they’ve been taught to want aren’t worth wanting at all?

Our Lady of Unrequited Lust

Played with delirious conviction by Vanessa Redgrave, Sister Jeanne is a hunchbacked nun whose devotion to God takes a backseat to her passion for Father Grandier (Oliver Reed).

Confined to a convent and ashamed of her body, Jeanne escapes into elaborate sexual fantasies about the handsome priest, imagining herself without her spinal deformity in a very public and passionate embrace. But Sister Jeanne doesn’t just want Grandier. She wants him to want her, and her conviction that he never will drives her toward increasingly destructive delusions.

In the renewed online conversation surrounding “The Devils,” most of the overt thirst has understandably been reserved for Reed’s rakish priest. “I would let Father Grandier do unspeakable things to me,” declared one of many, many Reddit users speaking to that theme.

Redgrave’s simultaneously sympathetic and villainous Sister Jeanne has inspired a more complicated fascination. “Sister Jeanne was the first femcel,” proclaimed one Letterboxd user after an October 17 screening.

Fifty-five years after her cinematic debut, Jeanne has become something like the patron saint of femcels. She’s lonely, sexually frustrated, and painfully conscious of her perceived undesirability. She’s also manipulative, vindictive, and complicit in a man’s destruction. Redgrave refuses to make either side easy to dismiss. Jeanne’s longing is pitiable, but its consequences are appalling.

Russell, however, is interested in more than watching a woman go mad with desire. Jeanne’s accusations of demonic possession become politically useful to authorities determined to destroy Grandier, transforming her private anguish into an elaborate public performance. Even as she helps persecute the object of her obsession, Jeanne is herself raped under the guise of an exorcism, subjected to invasive sexualized rituals by the very men exploiting her testimony. Her culpability doesn’t erase her victimhood, nor does her victimhood absolve her.

From the repressed Sister Ruth in “Black Narcissus” to the ostracized Carrie White and the desperately lonely heroine of “May,” horror has long made monsters of women whose desires exceed their circumstances. Their afflictions have been called everything from hysteria to demonic possession. Today, some viewers recognize them as cinematic femcels. (Hell, even Zendaya’s Emma in Kristoffer Borgli’s “The Drama” — a bullied teenager who once planned a school shooting — invites a more ideological reading of the archetype, her isolation having curdled into fantasies of violent revenge.)

Ironically, the term “incel” itself originated with a woman. In 1997, a queer Canadian known as Alana founded an inclusive online community for people struggling to find sex and romance. Over time, male-dominated forums appropriated the label, and Elliot Rodger’s 2014 killing spree in Isla Vista helped make it synonymous with violent misogyny. Some male incels even rejected the legitimacy of female romantic frustration, arguing that women could always obtain sex by lowering their standards.

Women helped create the language of romantic exclusion, only to find themselves excluded from it. Never mind that finding someone willing to sleep with you is hardly the same as finding someone who loves, respects, or even attracts you.

Nor are femcels simply female versions of violent male incels. A 2024 study by Hannah Rae Evans and Adam Lankford found that femcel discussions showed less support for aggression and violence than researchers had documented among male incels.

Then TikTok got involved. As researchers Jacob Johanssen and Jilly Boyce Kay explain, “femcelcore” transformed romantic exclusion into an often-ironic aesthetic of loneliness, resentment, self-loathing, and feminine rage. Literal femceldom and its more fashionable online performance are related but distinct phenomena, though popular culture increasingly treats them as interchangeable.

What began as an identity for women who felt fundamentally undesirable became an aesthetic that made their alienation seem desirable. Whether anyone is getting better at understanding them is another question.

The Monsters Men Make

Curry Barker’s “Obsession” takes the nightmare of unrequited love and turns it inside out.

Bear (Michael Johnston) is a romantically hopeless young man who uses a magical trinket to make his crush, Nikki (Inde Navarrette), fall hopelessly in love with him. It works a little too well. Nikki becomes the ultimate nightmare girlfriend: clingy, jealous, sexually insatiable, and eventually murderous. Her transformation recalls a long cinematic tradition of obsessive women, from “Fatal Attraction” to “Misery.”

But Barker’s clever reversal is that Nikki’s desires aren’t actually hers, and the monster is entirely of Bear’s making. Where Sister Jeanne’s authentic longing becomes a weapon for powerful men, Bear eliminates Nikki’s autonomy altogether. He wants the rewards of romance without the inconvenience of another person’s free will. Even after discovering the horrifying consequences of his wish, Bear struggles to relinquish control.

The real horror in “Obsession” isn’t a woman who loves too much, but a man who believes being loved is something he’s owed. Barker makes the violation literal when Bear has sex with Nikki after discovering that his wish has effectively imprisoned her inside her own body. The scene is rape, even if the enchanted version of Nikki appears willing. And her vacant, tearful expression makes clear that the real woman has no say in what’s happening to her.

Across five decades, “The Devils” and “Obsession” arrive at the same particularly ugly irony: Women portrayed as dangerous for wanting too much ultimately become victims of men who believe their bodies are available for the taking.

Actual femcels, meanwhile, appear considerably less frightening than their fictional counterparts. A 2026 study by Brandon Sparks and Alexandra Zidenberg compared 61 self-identified femcels with 58 other women, finding elevated levels of sexual depression, anxiety, and dissatisfaction among the former. Particularly striking was their fear of abuse by potential partners. The small, demographically uneven samples limit broader conclusions, but the irony is difficult to ignore: While horror imagines sexually frustrated women as people to fear, some of the real women behind the label are themselves afraid of being hurt.

Plus, loneliness doesn’t necessarily mean desperation. According to Pew Research Center, only 35 percent of single American women were actively looking for a relationship or casual dates in 2022, compared with half of single men. Enjoying single life and having other priorities were among the leading explanations offered by single Americans who weren’t looking. Not every woman without a partner considers herself deprived of one.

That distinction became politically charged after Donald Trump’s reelection in 2024, when some American women expressed interest in South Korea’s 4B movement, which rejects dating men, heterosexual marriage, sex with men, and childbirth. Born from feminist resistance to misogyny and sexual violence, 4B treats abstention not as romantic failure but as an exercise of autonomy. Its American visibility hardly established a mass exodus from heterosexuality, but it revealed something about the appeal of opting out.

Here, the language of femceldom begins to break down. Women who want relationships but cannot find them aren’t the same as women who no longer consider those relationships worth pursuing. Amid growing discussions of “heteropessimism,” or disillusionment with the promises of heterosexuality, the difference between being unwanted and refusing to participate matters more than ever.

And for a genre that has spent decades imagining women’s unsatisfied desires as a threat, that opens up some interesting possibilities.

What If She Never Wants Him?

For Kris Williams (Hannah Einbinder), the object of her obsession is already a horror movie.

In Jane Schoenbrun’s “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,” the young queer director is hired to revive a slasher franchise she’s worshipped since childhood. Her first priority is finding Billy Presley (Gillian Anderson), the reclusive actress who played its original final girl. Kris has spent years experiencing desire at a safe remove, through other people’s images. Meeting Billy threatens to collapse the distance between watching and wanting.

Like Sister Jeanne, she’s fixated on someone seemingly beyond her reach. Unlike Jeanne, she might actually get to find out what happens next.

The franchise has its own messy history. Once protested by the religious right, “Camp Miasma” is now considered transphobic, thanks to its gender-nonconforming killer. Enter Kris, hired to give the aging property a suitably progressive makeover. Yesterday’s moral panic is today’s branding opportunity.

Schoenbrun’s satire cuts in both directions. The studio cares little about the franchise’s ugliness or its pleasures, beyond whatever might make a reboot profitable. Kris, inconveniently, understands that making something politically acceptable isn’t necessarily the same as understanding its appeal.

This tension extends beyond Schoenbrun’s fictional studio. Barker’s “Obsession” has earned more than $520 million worldwide, compared with roughly $8.7 million for “Camp Miasma.” Their vastly different theatrical releases make those grosses an imperfect referendum on audience tastes, but the disparity illustrates how differently the industry markets stories about desire. Female obsession is profitable. Female autonomy is a harder pitch.

Billy knows more about that distinction than her admirer realizes. She reveals that an encounter previously understood as sex was, for her, an experience of sexual violence. The fantasy Kris treasured as a fan means something very different to the woman who lived it. Suddenly, the gap between the image and the person inside it becomes impossible to ignore.

Schoenbrun doesn’t suggest that desire can erase trauma. Instead, Kris and Billy’s growing intimacy makes room for something transformative: the freedom to explore fantasies without surrendering the right to decide what happens to their bodies. For once, the question isn’t whether a woman wants too much, but whether she gets to decide what she wants in the first place.

There’s a visual kinship with Russell, too. Derek Jarman’s blinding white architecture makes “The Devils” a cathedral of repression, while Schoenbrun’s candy-colored gore and hand-painted backdrops turn “Camp Miasma” into an ecstatic playground. Both directors abandon realism to give desire a world of its own.

But where Russell’s world turns longing into persecution, Schoenbrun lets it become a creative force. When Kris’s increasingly personal ideas clash with the studio’s plans, it looks less like a defeat than a beginning. Reclaiming horror, it turns out, might require more than giving an old franchise a new coat of paint.

Female rage became a lucrative entertainment category by making women’s anger legible as power.
