Femcelcore sells something slipperier: the misery of being unwanted as an identity other people might actually desire. Neither transformation settles the question of who profits from women’s pain, much less who gets to control its meaning.

For Sister Jeanne, wanting a man she cannot have becomes the engine of her destruction. For Nikki, being wanted by a man who refuses to accept her autonomy is just as catastrophic. Kris and Billy offer a more liberating possibility: desire needn’t end in possession, punishment, or even the conventional romance women have spent centuries being told to pursue.

The point isn’t that horror needs to become gentler, or that its ugliest fantasies should disappear. It’s that women deserve the freedom to make, watch, and reclaim these movies on their own terms.

It’s easy to picture Kris and Billy taking in a screening of “The Devils” on date night. But would they recognize themselves in Sister Jeanne? Pity her? Laugh at her? Maybe they’d just admire Russell’s outrageous imagery. Either way, the thought of two women, on a date, watching a nun want too much — and enjoying themselves immensely — feels like heaven.

From Warner Bros. Clockwork, “Ken Russell’s The Devils” is in theaters now.

entry.title: Walter Koenig, Actor Who Played Chekov on ‘Star Trek,’ Dies at 90
entry.summary: Walter Koenig, who played Anton Chekov on ‘Star Trek,' dies at 90.
entry.content:
Walter Koenig, who played Pavel Andreievich Chekov, a key member of the U.S.S. Enterprise on the original “Star Trek” series and across the first seven films, has died. He was 90.

As Chekov, a Russian crew member, Koenig spoke in a thick, almost exaggerrated accent and sported a Davy Jones “moptop”. His presence on the bridge was a reminder of Gene Roddenberry’s utopian vision. The original “Star Trek” aired during the height of the Cold War, but it imagined a future in which such regional conflicts had ended in the name of space exploration. Koenig first joined the starship in the show’s second season and would go on to appear in 36 episodes. He would later voice now-President Chekov in 2023’s “Star Trek: Picard.”

Related Stories
How ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York’ Used Vintage ‘Godfather’ Lenses to Capture NYC on Location
‘Queen at Sea’ Review: Juliette Binoche Guides Director Lance Hammer Back to Screens with a Searing Film About Dementia and Consent

On the big screen, Chekov was usually a bit player, though he did play a key role in “Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan.” His character’s scouting trip ends with Khan (Ricardo Montalbán) freed from exile and back in control of a space vessel.

Koenig’s film credits include “Goodbye, Raggedy Ann” and “Babylon 5.” In addition to acting, Koenig was a screenwriter who worked on such shows as “Land of the Lost,” “Family,” and “What Really Happened to the Class of ’65?.” He wrote several memoirs and was appeared frequently at Star Trek conventions.

“I was always very pleased when we were shooting the show and the motion pictures, to be identified with ‘Star Trek,'” Koenig said in a 2020 interview with Trekmovie.com. “I thought we were putting forward some very trenchant socio-political philosophies that needed to be articulated. I think we did that by projecting problems that were current into the future where it was more admissible. I was always pleased that we were dealing with issues of mankind and humanity and how we can achieve a better moral society and be inclusive of all races, creeds, sexes, philosophies, etcetera.”

entry.title: How ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York’ Used Vintage ‘Godfather’ Lenses to Capture NYC on Location
entry.summary: DP Sam Levy tells IndieWire about designing a throwback look for "The Only Living Pickpocket in New York" with the help of some vintage lenses.
entry.content:
John Turturro and cinematographer Sam Levy hadn’t worked together before, both signing onto Noah Segan’s “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” but they did have something in common. Levy came up as a camera assistant under the great Harris Savides, who also shot Turturro in “Margot at the Wedding.” They’d both gotten close to Savides and had all kinds of stories that gave the actor and DP a nice shared language to work on this throwback crime thriller about a thief named Harry (Turturro) who steals from the wrong vape goon (Will Price) and has one last, desperate chance to make good.

But Levy also had something tangible.

Related Stories
‘Queen at Sea’ Review: Juliette Binoche Guides Director Lance Hammer Back to Screens with a Searing Film About Dementia and Consent
‘Clayface’ Tops the Box Office with $24 Million. What Does It Signal About DC Studios’ Latest Reboot?

“The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” was shot primarily with a set of Bausch & Lomb Super Baltar lenses — the same set, in fact, that cinematographer Gordon Willis used to shoot “The Godfather.” But Savides also owned an even older set of original Baltar lenses that Levy brought to bless the set. “I carried Harris’ lenses with us,” Levy told IndieWire. “They’re very similar but had just a little bit of a different flavor, and they had a different focal length. Some of them had kind of in-between focal lengths. So, it was convenient, but it also just felt nice to have a piece of Harris.”

It’s especially nice for the eyes of the project, the lenses, to have history and lineage on a movie like “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York.” Segan’s thriller takes as its central dramatic question the tension between the analog and the digital, the New York that’s coming into being in the 2020s and the New York that’s disintegrating to bring it to life. And Levy really wanted to lean into that, visually.

“[The Super Baltars] have these aberrations in them which put off a lot of people. They vignette and they flare in a way that is very beautiful but you can’t — it’s hard [to control. For example, if you shoot with the iris wide open, they completely fall apart, and they look soft, but not in a pleasing way. Harris Savides used them on ‘Margot at the Wedding,’ which John is in. And at that time, I remember having a lot of conversations with [Savides] about how difficult they were,” Levy said.

But after doing some camera tests with Turturro and seeing how he looked through those lenses, Levy found a sweet spot that’s weathered and alluring, with a clarity that is purposeful but never too sharp or soulless. The flaws and the aberrations the lenses created were, in fact, Levy’s favorite parts. “It’s an urgent necessity to take risks when you’re a cinematographer and to try things that are maybe on the edge of being too dark or underexposed. I played a lot with that in this film, with silhouette,” Levy said.

This is especially true in the Bronx apartment that Harry shares with his wife Rosie (Karina Arroyave), trapped in a hospital bed in what New Yorker realtors would call a “prewar” building and what most New Yorkers would call “don’t trust that elevator to work.” Levy spent a lot of time there, trying to see and absorb the character of the space, not to correct it with lighting, but to see how it could help tell the story through how his camera captured it.

“ You open the door, you see the hallway; you close the door, it’s completely dark, and I knew so much happens in that little stretch. And I had to really spend time there to get to a place where it’s like, ‘Oh, when he comes home, he’ll emerge out of the darkness,” Levy said.

Levy also worked with production designer Rocío Giménez to arrange the space so we felt the transition and the invasion of Harry’s home when it happens. How can that conflict pop in the frame before the actors even start speaking?

“I suggested, ‘Why don’t we put a picture up and we see the guys in the reflection?’” Levy said. “It’s got to be at a very particular angle, and then we’ve got to light them so that you can really see [the goons in the next room], but we’re panning from John. It really was all in one. So that was really fun, but it was very painstaking to plot that out, and I worked very closely with Rocío Giménez, our great production designer, and our art director, Rosa Callejas, on being able to get that,” Levy said.

Giménez told IndieWire that her goal was to make sure Harry and Rosie’s apartment reflected a home that had history, and therefore room for all those hidden surprise angles, too. “It needed to feel textured — in the objects, in the layers of paint — and never remodeled. Things break, walls chip, and those marks accumulate over time. We also wanted the apartment to feel very warm, almost glowing. Although the apartment was a location, we transformed it extensively: reworking parts of the kitchen, adding wallpaper, repainting, and building walls to make the space feel smaller,” Giménez said.

Giménez and her team also made adjustments to make the home invasion look properly invasive, scattering even more objects around every time we cut back to it. But it took a real team effort to craft that sense of lived history that imbues every frame of “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” and especially those sequences in Harry’s apartment. Giménez, Levy, and Segan all talked about it extensively, and then, at a certain point, let their New York location have its say, too.

“When you’re working on a location — sometimes you don’t have the time, but it takes time to acclimate to the environment. And one thing I really learned from Harris Savides, that he would always say to me when, a few times, I got to operate for him, ‘Just look. Take a look at what you’re doing. Look at it. Don’t frame it up. Just sit there and look,’” Levy said.

It’s apt, then, that Savides’ lenses were on Turturro, right alongside Levy’s.

“The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” is now playing in theaters.

entry.title: ‘Queen at Sea’ Review: Juliette Binoche Guides Director Lance Hammer Back to Screens with a Searing Film About Dementia and Consent
entry.summary: Lance Hammer's first film in nearly two decades, 'Queen at Sea,' stars Juliette Binoche as the daughter of a dementia-addled woman. Review.
entry.content:
Editor’s Note: This review was originally published during the 2026 Berlin Film Festival. Greenwich Entertainment releases “Queen at Sea” in theaters starting Friday, October 30.

Lance Hammer was the toast of the town in 2008 with his hard-hitting, Mississippi-set coming-of-age drama “Ballast.” The Dardennes-esque vérité portrait of lives careening from loss and economic hardship won two awards at the Sundance Film Festival that year — including Best Director for Hammer — and received multiple Film Independent Spirit and Gotham award nominations.

And then, poof: Hammer was never heard from again.

He has now returned, almost two decades later, with an extremely upsetting but compassionate moral drama about agency amid dementia, titled “Queen at Sea.” It stars Juliette Binoche as a woman desperate and panicked to take care of her ailing mother, Leslie (Anna Calder-Marshall, absolutely shattering in her specificity toward the sickness’ toll), who is slipping deeper into the illness. Leslie’s grasp of time, memory, and function is vanishing in the multi-story London flat she shares with her husband of 19 years, Martin (a brutally heartbreaking Tom Courtenay). Meanwhile, Amanda (Binoche), an academic on sabbatical, is going through a separation herself — from her husband in Newcastle, and now she’s forced to bring her daughter, Sara (Florence Hunt), with her back to London to check in on her mother.

Related Stories

Box Office: A24’s ‘You Can See Everything’ Scores Huge $19.5 Million Second Weekend

But when Amanda catches her stepfather, Martin, in a compromising position with Leslie, another separation sets into motion, with Leslie potentially about to be lost in an elder-care system that’s frightening and scary for the patient, and a kind of emotional death sentence for her and her loved ones.

As someone who’s watched a close loved one lose themselves to Alzheimer’s disease, I found “Queen at Sea” to be especially bruising, even despite some of its patchier plot notes. The emotions are there, even if the story is, well, lost at sea at times. The geographical configuration surrounding Amanda, having left behind a husband (and Sara’s father) in Newcastle, is confusing. Meanwhile, Sara has very quickly restarted her life in Newcastle with new friends and a potential new flame, as writer/director Hammer draws parallel comparisons in the edit between Sara’s blooming relationship with a classmate, and Leslie’s mental deterioration and estrangement from her own partner.

When the movie begins, Amanda is on a house call to check on Leslie, and walks in on Martin attempting to have sex with a dazed-out, addled-eyed Leslie prostrate on the bed. This is not the first time this has happened, and it’s an occurrence Amanda has implored Martin to knock off. But the Viagra in his medicine cabinet suggests otherwise, that he keeps going back for more, that Amanda keeps asking him to stop.

Dementia dramas like Sarah Polley’s wounding “Away from Her” (wherein Julie Christie’s husband Grant Anderson basically sets her up in a nursing home to counteract his own infidelities) and Michael Haneke’s Oscar-winning “Amour” (the harshest of this fleet of films) tend to center close-up on the relations between an Alzheimer’s patient and her partner, and how these relationships break down when there are fewer past and present memories to found them on.

Hammer’s film introduces profound new questions and issues about consent into the formula — is Leslie agreeing on some level to have sex with her husband? Is the only pleasure in her winnowing life to be denied? Can a person with dementia consent to having sex? Leslie’s instincts now are narrowed to the primal: food, water, sleep, and, naturally, sex. So where do all these leftover feelings go when the body containing them is now only a vessel for a going mind?

Martin insists that Leslie — a once-celebrated and very talented painter now slowly going mute, mentally and emotionally and physically — is enjoying these encounters. They’ve been married for 19 years, after all, and when Amanda calls the police and introduces authorities into the situation, the couple is suddenly torn asunder. Then arise questions about whether they should continue to be separated and whether to place Leslie in a home.

Which is eventually what happens, and where Leslie forms an inappropriate bond with another patient to fill the Martin void. Writer/director Hammer, though, downplays the melodrama inherent to this scenario, even while shooting sequences, whether in Martin and Leslie’s apartment or in various hospitals, with a bracing handheld intimacy. (Cinematographer Adolpho Veloso, meanwhile, bathes London in a beautifully faded daylight.) Far from sterilely composed, a rape kit examination forced upon Leslie is harrowing and demeaning, especially as she has no idea what’s going on and no clue why a speculum is being inserted into her. In what world could Martin have raped his wife?

Binoche, who has been giving committed and emotionally controlled performances for years lately, including in films by Haneke, gives one of her most unsentimental and gripping performances at this stage in her career in “Queen at Sea.” An emotional phone call to her soon-to-be ex-husband lays bare to blanched vulnerability as she dials the last person she would prefer not to call, but the one she is forced to anyway. Interior lives outside those determined by this situation may be lacking, but Leslie’s isn’t. Amanda’s mother seems to activate when given the chance to paint at a nursing home, an aseptic and terrible place for which everyone in the family seems to be awkwardly auditioning.

The great British actor Courtenay, most recently memorable in the similarly memory-impaired marriage portrait “45 Years” opposite Charlotte Rampling, is quite devastating as a husband scrambling for answers and to legitimize his own place in Leslie’s life. The one element that doesn’t quite land, and seems quite literally chopped into the film, is Florence Hunt as Amanda’s daughter. Hammer seems to be trying to signal that she may be headed for her own future mental ruin by intercutting her first romance with scenes of Martin and Leslie’s last. It’s a noble idea, but it ends up feeling like scraps from an earlier draft.

Ultimately, though, anyone who’s endured what Amanda, or Leslie, or Martin do in this movie will find something to relate to and feel toward. Hammer spares no hard truths and offers no pat feelings with regard to how these people are bound to end up and what dementia ultimately does to them. Let’s just say hope is at a shortage. But the actors help carry Hammer’s message — and make it unforgettable.

Grade: B+

“Queen at Sea” premiered at the 2026 Berlin Film Festival. Greenwich Entertainment opens the film starting Friday, October 30.
